module_title: The Operative Portion, Costs, and Judicial Decorum
introduction: Tailored for Judicial Service Mains, this level explores the absolute climax of the judgment: the Operative Portion (Relief and Costs). It also details the strict rules of judicial decorum, explaining what judges are legally forbidden from writing in their judgments.

core_concepts.title: The Relief and Operative Portion
core_concepts.description:
The final paragraph of the judgment that commands action. It must be absolutely precise, unambiguous, and executable.
- It must state exactly who pays whom, how much, within what time, and what happens if they fail.
- Specificity: Never write 'The suit is decreed in favor of the plaintiff.' Write: 'The suit is decreed. The Defendant is directed to pay the Plaintiff a sum of ₹1,00,000/- along with pendente lite and future interest at 6% p.a. within 60 days from today.'

core_concepts.title: Awarding Costs (Section 35 & 35A, CPC)
core_concepts.description:
A civil judge must apply their mind to the costs of the litigation.
- The Golden Rule: **Costs shall follow the event**. This means the losing party must pay the legal costs of the winning party. 
- Exception: If the judge decides NOT to award costs to the winner, the judge is legally mandated to record reasons in writing for such a departure.
- Compensatory Costs (Sec 35A): If a party raises false or vexatious claims/defenses, the judge can impose special compensatory costs on them.

core_concepts.title: Judicial Decorum: Avoiding Sweeping Remarks
core_concepts.description:
The Supreme Court has issued strict guidelines on judgment writing (*State of U.P. v. Mohammad Naim*).
- The Rule: Judges must use sober, restrained language. They must NOT make disparaging, derogatory, or sweeping remarks against parties, witnesses, or government authorities unless it is strictly necessary for deciding the case. Unnecessary moralizing or philosophizing must be avoided.

core_concepts.title: Res Judicata and Issue Estoppel in Judgments
core_concepts.description:
How a judge writes their findings directly impacts future litigation.
- If a judge gives a definitive finding on an issue, it binds the parties forever (Res Judicata). Therefore, a judge should not make casual *obiter* comments on issues that are not strictly before them, as it may prejudice the parties in other pending litigations.

important_entities.name: Pendente Lite Interest (Section 34, CPC)
important_entities.key_fact: Interest awarded for the duration the suit was pending in court.
important_entities.significance: A critical part of the relief. A judge has the discretion to order interest from the date the suit was instituted until the date of the decree. In commercial transactions, this is usually awarded at the contractual rate; in non-commercial, it is typically capped at 6% per annum.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Can a judge award a relief that is perfectly just and fair, but was NEVER requested by the plaintiff in the plaint's 'Prayer' clause? **NO**. The Supreme Court strictly holds that *a court cannot grant a relief which is not claimed*. A judge's power is fenced by the prayer clause of the plaint.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: W W H T I C (Who, What, How much, Time, Interest, Costs)
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Before finalizing your judgment draft in the exam, ensure your operative paragraph answers: Who pays Who, What amount, within what Time limit, with what Interest, and what happens to the Costs.

exam_strategy_tips: In Judiciary Mains, missing the '(OPP)' or '(OPD)' tags while framing issues, or forgetting to explicitly address 'Costs' in the operative portion, will result in heavy penalization. Examiners look for these specific procedural markers.
